question.text:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(0,0), (2,0),(2,2).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of $S',$ the image of $S$ under a clockwise rotation of $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians about the origin?

  1. $(2,-2)$
  2. $\big(-1,-\sqrt{3}\big)$
  3. $\big(\sqrt{3},0\big)$
question.explanation:
The rotation matrix $R_\theta$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

\[ R_\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}. \]

Substituting $\theta = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ into the above, we have

\begin{align*} R &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) & -\sin\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\\ \sin\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) & \cos\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2}& \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\ -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}& -\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & \sqrt{3}\\ -\sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

To find the image of $S$ under the transformation, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} X &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 &2 \\ 0 &0 &2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the rotation $\mathbf{R}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} RX &= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & \sqrt{3}\\ -\sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 &2 \\ 0 &0 &2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2& (2\sqrt{3}-2) \\ 0& -2\sqrt{3}& (-2\sqrt{3}-2) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1& (\sqrt{3}-1) \\ 0& -\sqrt{3}& (-\sqrt{3}-1) \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of $S'$ are \[ (0,0), \quad \left(-1,-\sqrt{3}\right), \quad \left(\sqrt{3}-1,-\sqrt{3}-1\right). \]

So, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Rotating an Object About the Origin

question.text:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(-1,-1), (-1,2),(2,-3).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of $S',$ the image of $S$ under a clockwise rotation of $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ radians about the origin?

  1. $\big(0,\sqrt{2}\big)$
  2. $(3,-1)$
  3. $(-5,1)$
question.explanation:
The rotation matrix $R_\theta$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

\[ R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}. \] Substituting $\theta = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ into the above, we have \[ \begin{align*} R &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) & -\sin\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)\\ \sin\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) & \cos\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}& \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}& -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1\\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}\]

To find the image of $S$ under the transformation, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} X &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 &-1 & 2\\ -1 &2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*} \]

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the rotation $\mathbf{R}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{align*} RX &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1\\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 &-1 & 2\\ -1 &2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & -5\\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\\ \sqrt{2} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of $S'$ are \[ \left(0,\sqrt{2}\right), \quad \left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}},-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right), \quad \left( -\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right). \]

So, the correct answer is "I only."

example.title: Rotating an Object About the Origin

question.text:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(-2,0), (2,0),(0,2).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of $S',$ the image of $S$ under a clockwise rotation of $30^\circ$ about the origin?

  1. $\left(1,-\sqrt{3}\right)$
  2. $\big(1, \sqrt{3}\big)$
  3. $\left(\sqrt{3},-1\right)$
question.explanation:
The rotation matrix $R_\theta$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

\[ R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}. \]

Substituting $\theta = -30^\circ$ into the above, we have

\begin{align*} R &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos\left(-30^\circ\right) & -\sin\left(-30^\circ\right)\\[5pt] \sin\left(-30^\circ\right) & \cos\left(-30^\circ\right) \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}& \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] -\dfrac{1}{2} &\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & 1\\ -1 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

To find the image of $S$ under the transformation, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} X &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 &2& 0\\ 0 &0& 2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= 2\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1& 0\\ 0 &0& 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} \]

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the rotation $\mathbf{R}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{align*} RX &= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & 1\\ -1 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}\left(2 \begin{bmatrix} -1 &1& 0\\ 0 &0& 1 \end{bmatrix}\right)\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & 1\\ -1 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 &1& 0\\ 0 &0& 1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} &1 \\[3pt] 1 &-1 & \sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of $S'$ are

\[ \left(-\sqrt{3},1\right), \quad \left(\sqrt{3},-1\right),\quad \left(1,\sqrt{3}\right). \]

So, the correct answer is "II and III only."

example.title: Rotating an Object About the Origin

question.text:
What is the geometrical interpretation of the transformation represented by the matrix $A$ given below? 
\[
 A=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}&  \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\
 -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}& \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\
 \end{bmatrix}
 \]
question.explanation:
The rotation matrix $R_\theta$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

\[ R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \]

Comparing $A$ with the rotation matrix, we have

\[ \begin{cases} \sin\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\[3pt] \cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}. \end{cases} \]

Since $\cos\theta \gt 0$ and $\sin\theta \lt 0$ we must have that $\theta$ lies in $4$th quadrant.

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

\[ \tan\theta = -1. \] The principal value $\theta$ is \[ \theta= \arctan\left(-1 \right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \]

Therefore, $A$ represents a rotation of $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}$ radians clockwise about the origin.

question.text:
What is the geometrical interpretation of the transformation represented by the matrix $A$ given below? 
\[
 A=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}&  \dfrac{1}{2}\\
 -\dfrac{1}{2}& -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\
 \end{bmatrix}
 \]
question.explanation:
The rotation matrix $R_\theta$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta$ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

\[ R_\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}. \]

Comparing $A$ with the rotation matrix, we have

\[ \begin{cases} \sin\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\\[3pt] \cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. \end{cases} \]

Since $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ both are negative we must have $\pi \leq \theta\leq \dfrac{3\pi}{2} .$

Dividing the first equation by the second gives \[ \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}. \] The principal value $\theta_1$ is \[ \theta_1 = \arctan\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \] but this is outside the range $\pi \leq x \leq \dfrac {3\pi} 2.$ To find a value in the required range, we add $\pi\mathbin{:}$ \[ \theta = \theta_1 + \pi = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}. \] Therefore, our matrix represents a rotation of $\dfrac {7\pi} 6$ radians anticlockwise about the origin.

Finally, this is equivalent to a clockwise rotation with an angle of rotation given by

\[ 2\pi - \dfrac{7\pi}{6} =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ \dfrac {5\pi}{6}}. \]
